item.title: Trump hid in catering truck in secret plane swap over Iran threat, reports say
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2g90vvy62o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump hid in catering truck in secret plane swap over Iran threat, reports say - Published Donald Trump secretly swapped planes as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month, as part of an elaborate ruse in response to a possible Iranian threat, US media report. The US president boarded Air Force One in view of television cameras before being transported to a military aircraft with the help of a catering truck, the Washington Post said. Journalists and some White House staff on board did not know he had been smuggled out. Officials told the BBC's US partner CBS News that the US had detected a credible Iranian threat to fire a missile at the plane. The White House has not confirmed the secret switch. Trump had earlier said he was Iran's "number one target" during the summit in Ankara. The clandestine manoeuvre came a day after the US renewed military strikes on Iran following a breakdown of negotiations between Washington and Tehran to end the war. Trump had arrived in Turkey aboard a newer Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar, but announced that he would leave on the old Air Force One "for old time's sake". On 8 July, footage showed him boarding the presidential jet at Ankara airport. But according to the Washington Post, he was then secretly taken to a smaller C-32A military aircraft - a modified Boeing 757 often used by the vice-president - via a catering truck which had been elevated to plane level on the opposite side to where he had boarded. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth boarded the C-32A separately using external stairs in an effort to make the flight appear normal, according to the newspaper. Journalists and some White House staff boarded Air Force One and were reportedly told to close their window shades. They were unaware the president was no longer on board. A pool producer who was on the plane said one unusual moment on the flight was the request that members of the press keep the shades down. A photographer briefly opened one and was quickly told to close it and that it was a request from the Secret Service, which guards the president. The producer, in a report from the White House Correspondents Association provided on Tuesday, also noted there appeared to have been two catering trucks at both the front and back of the plane when the press arrived, and their van had been too far back in the motorcade at the airport be able to take a photo of the president boarding. Technically "Air Force One" is the call sign for any aircraft carrying the US president. But on this occasion, the C-32A used the call sign "Reach 18", while the aircraft carrying the journalists continued to use "AF1" in order to keep up the ruse. Trump then flew to the UK en route to the US, where he reboarded the old Air Force One and was seen descending from the aircraft after it landed at RAF Mildenhall. It is unclear how he moved from the C-32A back to the legacy jet. The president then transferred to the new Qatari-donated Air Force One to travel back to Washington. During that flight, Trump spoke to reporters on board where he noted the threats posed by Iran but did not mention the earlier plane swap. Asked why reporters had been told to lower the window shades on the plane from Turkey, Trump said: "Because you're probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags we have to deal with." He said he had a "threat all the time" on his life, and that he is "number one" on Iran's "list". "But if I go, you go, right?", he said, adding: "Perhaps someday you want to change professions." White House communications director Steven Cheung did not directly confirm or deny the reports, but said the new Air Force One was a "state-of-the-art aircraft" fitted with security measures to protect the president and his staff. US intelligence had previously warned of a specific threat of an attack on Trump or his aircraft, according to earlier reporting by CBS News. The New York Times previously reported on security concerns regarding the Qatari-gifted jet, including that the Secret Service had urged Trump to switch planes on his return from the Nato summit. Several of the publication's journalists were summoned to testify under oath in response. The Justice Department subsequently told the BBC that it was investigating illegal leaks. The US has spent months retrofitting the $400m Boeing 747-8 to prepare it for the president. Older Air Force One planes have laser technology to blind incoming missiles, sources have told CBS News. It is unclear what systems the Qatari jet has. "The new Air Force One is perfectly safe for the president's travels, but will receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall which will take approximately one month to complete," White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in a statement to CBS News. item.title: Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c151dpzwnvxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says - Published Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles. Ukraine said strikes on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia - which killed seven people and injured at least 24 - involved ballistic missiles from Russia's ally. In Voronezh, western Russia, warehouses of the biggest online retailer Wildberries were hit by Ukraine. The company, known as Russia's Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks. The attacks come a day after at least 13 people were killed, including one child, in Ukrainian drone strikes on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, more than 1,100 km (680 miles) from the Ukrainian border. In a video address on Monday evening, Zelensky said "for the first time" Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea". "The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots", Zelensky said, adding that this poses a danger to the rest of the world. He has not presented any evidence to back up his comments. It is not the first time Zelensky as well as other senior Ukrainian and Western officials have accused Russia of receiving military assistance from North Korea. Ukraine's military has said that says dozens of North Korean missiles have been fired by Russia into its territory since Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The Ukrainian president warned over the weekend that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight with Russian forces. Some 11,000 North Korean soldiers were deployed to help Moscow push Ukrainian troops out of the western Russian region of Kursk following their cross-border incursion in August 2024. In January 2025, Western officials told the BBC that North Korean troops had suffered nearly 40% casualties in the fighting there in just three months. In his Monday's address, Zelensky also hailed a successful air strike on a Russian petrochemical plant in western Siberia on Monday as a "very significant achievement" by the Ukrainian military. He promised "more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary". Zaporizhzhia regional head Ivan Fedorov posted photos of vehicles and buildings on fire, saying Moscow had struck the city using missiles and guided bombs. All seven casualties were employees of Ukraine's Zaporizhstal metallurgical plant, which later halted all its operations. One person was injured in strikes on the capital Kyiv, where air raid sirens sounded twice during the night. Explosions could be heard on the outskirts of the capital, triggering fires. Local officials later said a children's hospital was damaged - but there were no injuries as staff and patients were sheltering. Two women have been injured in a Russian drone strike on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Sumy, according to regional head Serhii Kryvosheienko. He later said that one person was killed when Russia attacked the city with gliding bombs in the afternoon. Meanwhile, strikes on substations in Kherson and Kharkiv resulted in power outages. Ukrainian officials say Russia fired 120 drones overnight and a range of different missiles, but for the first time they have not given a number of missiles fired or intercepted. It follows an Air Force statement on Monday urging the media not to write "sensationalised headlines" or "spread pessimism" about the shortage of air defence interceptors. Separately, there have been reports of a fire and explosions at a logistics centre of Wildberries in the Voronezh region. Wildberries has not yet confirmed the attack, but said that its facilities in the region, which borders Ukraine, have been evacuated. In July, Ukrainian drone attacks on several retail warehouses belonging to Wildberries disrupted the operations of a large number of small and medium-sized Russian businesses. Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army. The attack on Tatarstan this week was one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. At least 75 people were injured in the strikes, with Ukraine's Armed Forces saying it had hit the city's Tanevo oil refinery. Verified images on social media showed large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background. The Uzbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan. Related topics - Published1 day ago - Published5 days ago

item.title: Ousted Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death in absentia
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce34dkpnyg7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ousted Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death in absentia - Published A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war. It is the first conviction against Assad, who fled from Damascus to the Russian capital, Moscow, with his family after his regime was overthrown in December 2024, ending his family's five-decade grip on power. Assad's cousin and the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province, Atef Najib, was also sentenced to death. He appeared wearing a striped prison uniform inside a cage in the courtroom as the judge read out his sentence. Deraa is widely seen as the birthplace of the uprising against Assad's rule. In March 2011, the detention and alleged torture of a group of teenagers accused of writing anti-government graffiti sparked protests in the city, which were met with a violent crackdown by security forces. That response helped ignite nationwide demonstrations that escalated into civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed. Syria's interim government began trying officials associated with the Assad regime, which ruled the country for more than 50 years, earlier this year. Najib is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial. He was convicted of crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15" and "torture leading to death". The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death, including Bashar al-Assad's younger brother, Maher. He ran the army's elite Fourth Division and also fled to Moscow when the regime fell. The others convicted include former defence minister Fahd al-Freij. Outside the courthouse after the ruling, hundreds of people of all ages gathered holding pictures of their loved ones who were killed by the regime. Crowds were clapping and chanting, while cars drove by excitedly honking their horns. A group of men passed out flags. "The joy is indescribable," one man told the BBC, hoisting up a photo of his late father. "God willing we will see Bashar al-Assad and all his aides hanging on the gallows." Another woman told the BBC everyone is feeling a mix of "victory and liberation." "The voices of the victims are finally heard. Justice has been achieved!" she exclaimed. Nouha al-Masri, a prosecutor in the case, lost her brother during the March 2011 crackdown and massacre at al-Omari Square in Deraa. "We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us," Masri told the BBC. "Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward." - Syria trial seen as first step on long road for Assad's victims - Published29 April - The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding - Published3 days ago - Calls for justice and accountability in Syria grow after Assad's fall - Published6 January 2025 It remains unclear whether Syria's new authorities will be able to secure Bashar and Maher al-Assad's extraditions from Moscow. It is not the first move against Assad by Syria's new leadership. An arrest warrant was issued against him last December on charges of murder and torture. He left for Russia as forces under Ahmed al-Sharaa - now Syria's president - swept to power in a rapid, 11-day campaign that brought down the Assad dynasty. Since then, the new government has detained numerous former officials and security personnel, though most senior figures from the old regime, including Assad himself, remain out of reach in Russia. Attempts by Syrian opposition figures to pursue Assad through courts in Western countries during the final years of his rule did not lead to any convictions. Assad came to power in 2000 after the death of his father. The second son of Hafez al-Assad, he was not destined to be Syria's ruler until his brother, Basil, died in a car crash in 1994. Part of the Alawite minority, he continued to favour their dominance in many roles in the military, security and intelligence agencies. Much of his rule was defined by the civil war. Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus and Leen Alsaadi, BBC Arabic in Deraa. Related topics - Published9 December 2024

item.title: Russia releases former US Marine reported in poor health
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgj4m8e1ryo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Russia releases former US Marine reported in poor health - Published President Donald Trump said a US Marine held in a Russian prison, whose health was reportedly in extremely poor condition, has been released. "After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that no prisoner swap took place. In 2022, Gilman, who is from Massachusetts, was arrested for allegedly kicking a police officer while aboard a train. He had recently been moved from prison to a civilian hospital in Russia after going into a catatonic-like state. Trump said the 32-year-old was on a flight back to the US accompanied by his mother, doctors, and members of the administration. According to a statement from his family, Gilman is expected to later arrive at a US military hospital in Texas where he will be assessed and treated. His health was in "life-threatening condition" after he was subjected to "harsh and abusive treatment", the family said. "The Russians treated my brother so badly. They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both and American and a Marine," his sister, Lexi Hudson, said in the statement. "I am so grateful to President Trump for saving my brother's life," she added. Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey also helped secure her brother's release, she said. In a statement, Markey said: "Approximately 50 days ago, Robert was diagnosed with a dissociative stupor - a condition where he is non-responsive and unable to interact or eat. " In Russian confinement, Gilman was subject to repeated harassment, including forced exercise training sessions that lasted up to 16 hours and the administration of psychotropic drugs, Eric Lebson, who advocated for Gilman's release as part of the group Global Reach, told CBS News, the BBC's media partner. The abuse was so severe that at one point Gilman had required a feeding tube in his nose, according to Lebson. Gilman served in the US Marines from August 2019 to August 2020. He was arrested for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk aboard a train to Moscow in January 2022 and was initially given a sentence of three and a half years. He was later found guilty of assaulting prison guards, after he allegedly attacked a prison inspector during a cell check. His sentence was then increased to 10 years. Lebson said five other Americans remain in Russia, each contending with medical issues. Their names are Aleksandr Antonov, David Barnes, Olga Jezler, Andre Khachatoorian, and Chuck Zimmerman.

item.title: Watch: Family escapes home during Colombia earthquake
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cwyl3w1e6zxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Watch: Family escapes home during Colombia earthquake A family captured video of the moment they fled their home during an earthquake in Colombia. Liliana Pérez Ocampo and her family escaped moments before their home was rocked by a 7.4 magnitude quake on Monday. "At first, we thought it was just a mild tremor like the ones that usually happen in Colombia, but when more than 30 seconds passed and everything was shaking harder, we realised it was an earthquake," the mother-of-four told the BBC World Service. Her family, including two young children at school, are safe. "In the end, material things can be replaced," she said. "The most important thing is life, and we have that." With at least 169 people killed, this has been the strongest earthquake to hit Colombia in the 21st Century, according to the country's Geological Service. item.title: Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8enj8p1xwgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty - Published Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country in the Middle East to formally end capital punishment. A majority of MPs in the 128-seat parliament backed the measure on Tuesday, while Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voted against it. The legislation will now go to the cabinet before being passed to President Joseph Aoun for signing. The government has already expressed its support for the measure. Lebanon has not carried out an execution since January 2004, although courts have continued to hand down death sentences. Rights groups estimate that more than 78 people remain on death row. Under the new legislation, capital punishment will be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour. However, the legislation does not yet set out in detail how the new sentence would be enforced. Hard labour is already written into Lebanese law but has rarely been implemented in recent years. The country's financial crisis and overcrowded prisons have limited the authorities' resources and capacity. The latest legislation follows years of campaigning by civil society groups and lawyers for the removal of capital punishment from Lebanese law. "We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," Oragit Younan told the BBC. As co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights, she led a nearly three-decade campaign to abolish the death penalty in Lebanon. "We are in a war, and people [have been] killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win. We can be a model for others," she said. Tuesday's vote in parliament follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions. An execution required a decree signed by the president, prime minister and justice minister - but no such decree has been signed since 2004. Under Lebanese law, the death penalty could previously be imposed for some of the country's most serious offences, including aggravated murder, certain terrorism-related crimes resulting in death, treason, espionage and offences against state security. Previous attempts to abolish the death penalty have failed, including legislation introduced in parliament in 2004 and a proposal from the justice ministry in 2008. Lebanon's move comes as the use of the death penalty remains contested elsewhere in the Middle East. Jordan resumed executions in June, carrying out its first since 2017. In Israel, its parliament has approved legislation that allows for the expansion of the circumstances in which capital punishment can be imposed. Israeli MPs passed a new law in May to impose the death penalty and conduct public trials for those involved in the Hamas-led attacks and mass hostage-taking in Israel in October 2023. Elsewhere, the UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear among the population and suppress dissent". In Iran, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said earlier this month.

item.title: France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy5d11g72ppo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls - Published France has banned unsolicited telemarketing phone calls, in what a consumer group is hailing as a "small revolution" for the sales industry. From Tuesday, unsolicited calls are prohibited for businesses in all sectors - but there are some exceptions. Calls will only be permitted if they relate to a contract a person has already entered into or the company has obtained prior consent to be contacted for marketing. "It cannot be stressed enough that peace and quiet is a right, and it is time to stop exposing consumers to unwanted solicitations," consumer advocacy group Que Choisir Ensemble, said in a statement. "This observation also holds true online and on the street, which are saturated with demands to consume," group president Marie-Amandine Stévenin added. She said the group had long been advocating "for an end to the automatic assumption that someone in their home or private life is a potential customer." "This is a victory for consumers, the vast majority of whom do not want to receive sales calls," she said. But the law change has riled some business groups, and officials in Morocco, where the call centre sector is heavily reliant on the French market. One government minister estimated the telemarketing restrictions could lead to the loss of up to 50,000 jobs, according to a report in Moroccan newspaper Le Matin. The head of France's direct-selling trade association, the Fédération de la Vente Directe (FVD), also criticised the reforms for adding what he said were administrative burdens for businesses. "You'll have to obtain written consent from your customer, and you'll also have to keep proof of that consent," Frédéric Billon said in comments reported by the New York Times. According to a 2025 parliamentary report, 97% of people are annoyed by telemarketing calls, with the authors wryly noting it is "one of those rare issues that unites people in France". The same report found 72% of French people reported being contacted on their mobile phones at least once a week, while 38% said they were called once a day. Germany, Austria and Italy are among the European countries that impose significant restrictions on telemarketing calls, often referred to as cold calls. In the UK, most telemarketing calls are legal provided the recipient has not objected to the call and their number is not on a statutory list of people or businesses who do not want to receive calls. item.title: Former judge removed by Orbán elected Hungarian president
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyed7rem5no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Former judge removed by Orbán elected Hungarian president - Published Hungary's parliament has elected András Baka, 73, a respected judge and former head of the Supreme Court, as head of state. The Hungarian president is a largely figurehead role, but Baka's rule promises to be tempestuous. His task will be to monitor Prime Minister Péter Magyar's efforts to dismantle the interlocking economic and political powerhouse established by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. He will also oversee the writing of a new constitution, to replace Orbán's constitution of 2011. "We cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," András Baka told Parliament, after he was elected by 140 votes to 6. "The majority of society now feels a sense of liberation and hope. Others feel disappointment and uncertainty," he said. "In a democratic society, this is not an anomaly, but a natural state of affairs." All 51 MPs belonging to Orbán's party Fidesz walked out of the chamber before the vote, in protest against the ousting of their favourite, Tamás Sulyok, from the post last month. In his speech, András Baka promised the broadest possible debate on the creation of a new constitution. Since taking office in early May, the new Magyar government has lost no time attacking Orbán's legacy. Twenty-seven laws have been passed, and two amendments to the constitution. The states of emergency - migrants, Covid, and war in Ukraine - which Orbán used to govern by decree, were all cancelled. The Sovereignty Protection Office, which the Fidesz government used to attack critical journalists and NGOs, was abolished, and an National Asset Recovery and Protection Office was established, with sweeping powers to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of stealing state funds under the former government. Fidesz accuses the Tisza government of establishing a "tyranny". Ironically, they removed Baka from his post as president of the Supreme Court in 2011, for attempting to stop them undermine the rule of law. Public service radio and TV have been off air since 9 July, as news programmes are revamped. The stated aim is to restore their independence, from their Fidesz-era role as government propaganda organs. Other key changes came under Amendments 16 and 17 of the constitution, limiting the prime minister to two terms in office, and MPs to three. The ability of the Constitutional Court to oversee acts of parliament, taken away by Fidesz, was also restored. If the Tisza majority expects Baka to be a tame president, they may get a rude awakening. In a BBC interview before he was asked to take the post, he made clear he opposes the limitation of MPs' terms as an intrusion on the right of voters to freely choose their representatives. Baka served for 17 years as the Hungarian judge at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. "I am not a political man," he told the BBC last month. "I got involved in politics through my professional, legal way of thinking." Baka was elected today as a transitional figure. Under the constitutional amendment which made his presidency possible, the new president will likely only be in place until the new constitution comes into force - or for maximum of five years. Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, Baka made it clear that he intended to push back against the Hungarian tendency to trust in powerful leaders. "The state is not there for itself," he said, at the end of his speech. "It is there for the people." Related topics - Published14 April - Published13 April

item.title: Luigi Mangione appears in court as questions remain in case ahead of murder trial
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgje05wd1v4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Luigi Mangione appears in court as questions remain in case ahead of murder trial - Published The judge overseeing the state trial of Luigi Mangione, the man accused of killing UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson, has laid down the ground rules for court public and media access to the high-profile case. Mangione returned to court on Tuesday ahead of his murder trial, which begins next month in New York. The case has attracted national attention, and has also created an online frenzy, with both his backers - many of whom see Mangione as a symbol of the backlash against US healthcare costs - and his critics analysing everything from his intentions to his appearance. The spectacle is likely to intensify when jury selection for the trial begins on 8 September. Mangione, if found guilty, could face decades behind bars. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including second-degree murder and weapons-related offences. He faces a separate federal trial next year, in which he has also pleaded not guilty. Much of what is expected at the state trial – the prosecutor's case, Mangione's defence, and obstacles both parties face – were previewed in months of court filings and arguments, but some questions remain unanswered. Will the prosecution win battle over evidence? One of the most crucial elements of the Mangione case was decided earlier this summer, after a multi-day hearing in December where the judge weighed which evidence prosecutors could present during trial. Mangione's team mounted an aggressive bid to exclude evidence recovered from his Pennsylvania arrest. It alleged that state police improperly seized and searched Mangione's possessions, and did not properly advise him of his constitutional rights before questioning him. The defence succeeded in excluding some items, including a gun magazine, cell phone, passport, wallet and computer chip found in Mangione's backpack. But Judge Gregory Carro allowed at trial a gun and notebook with Mangione's purported writings, viewed as vital to the prosecution. Prosecutors have unveiled surveillance footage showing the moment Thompson was shot from behind by a hooded individual. They also used footage to piece together Mangione's alleged movements after the shooting, and ballistics and fingerprint evidence they claim bolsters their case. What might Mangione's defence look like? As trial approaches, Mangione's team has yet to unveil its full strategy. So far, his lawyers have not offered a robust alternative theory to the one prosecutors have put forth. "We do not have, like in 'The Fugitive,' the idea of the one-armed man who's the real killer," said former federal prosecutor Mitchell Epner, referencing a 1993 thriller about a man wrongly convicted of killing his wife. Earlier this summer, Mangione's lawyers proposed, then quickly withdrew, an "extreme emotional disturbance" argument. In such a defence, New York law requires lawyers to show a defendant "acted under the influence of extreme emotional disturbance for which there was a reasonable explanation or excuse". Extreme emotional disturbance would allow the jury to consider the less severe charge of manslaughter, rather than second-degree murder. But jurors would have to be convinced of the accused's state of mind at the time. Some experts wondered if Mangione would argue a full insanity plea - different from emotional disturbance, but his lawyers have not proposed it. "Short of being delusional, or having no understanding of the nature of what one is doing, an insanity defence is not likely to be successful," said Cheryl Bader, who leads the Criminal Defence Clinic at the Fordham University School of Law. Mangione's team did not immediately respond to a request for comment. As in every US criminal trial, the burden rests on the prosecution to prove its case to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt, a high legal bar. "The more his case is about the question of who killed the victim, the easier it is for the prosecution," said Epner. Epner cited other themes, including healthcare in America, as potential narrative threads that could sway a jury in Mangione's favour. "The more it's about the other peripheral issues, the harder it is for the prosecution," he said. Who will be able to watch? In recent weeks, Mangione's lawyers and prosecutors have traded terse court filings debating just how much access the public will have to the trial. The trial is expected to generate coverage across traditional outlets, social media, and streaming platforms. Mangione's supporters have demanded more transparency, and frequently post and broadcast from outside court. On Tuesday, Carro said the court would open an overflow room during the trial, which will allow more members of the public and press to attend in person. In earlier court filings, Mangione's lawyers had questioned the court's press procedures, and why the court had not yet established an overflow room to meet public demand. They also implied – and later walked back – that prosecutors were influencing the court's media policies, which the Manhattan District Attorney's office denied. Carro took to the bench to rebuke Mangione's attorneys for their filings, saying "any suggestion the district is involved is simply incorrect". He also chastised prosecutors for raising security concerns about an overflow room, telling them it was not the court's "first rodeo" with blockbuster cases. While the public can be admitted to court in New York, space is often limited at high-profile trials. The court and its press office "remain firmly committed to providing the greatest possible access for both the media and the public", spokesman Al Baker said, adding that the court is "evaluating the complex logistical and safety considerations involved". item.title: Houthis reportedly kill four in first deadly attack since start of Iran war
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg9wpmzmlno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Houthis reportedly kill four in first deadly attack since start of Iran war - Published Four people have reportedly been killed in an attack on a small cargo ship in the Red Sea suspected to have been carried out by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, the internationally recognised government of Yemen has said. If confirmed, it would be the first deadly strike by the group on a vessel since the US and Israel started a conflict against Iran. Yemen's transport ministry said the ship was hit with three ballistic missiles, south of the port of Mocha, causing a fire on board and resulting in the deaths of four crew - three Pakistanis and one Indonesian. The Houthis began attacks on shipping last month - announcing a naval blockade of Saudi ports. They have not admitted carrying out the attack. The conflict in the region has been ongoing since the end of February, punctuated by a faltering ceasefire which was meant to lead to a deal to end the war. It has whipped up regional tensions, with the Houthis also attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and oil facilities, in parallel with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway where a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit. The attack comes after a years-long truce in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government collapsed last month. The Houthis control much of north-western Yemen, and frequently clash with the government. The government operates out of Aden in the south, due to the capital Sanaa being held by the Houthis. Social media images examined by BBC Verify appear to show a damaged cargo ship in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which sits at the inlet of the Red Sea, off the coast of Yemen. In its statement, the Yemeni government said the ship had been carrying food, and that the attack on a commercial vessel marked an escalation in approach from the Houthis. In an earlier statement, maritime risk management company Vanguard said the Yemeni Navy deployed to assist the vessel and came under fire. This resulted in three others being injured. Close-up pictures show the vessel is named Tihamah which, according to ship-tracking platform MarineTraffic, is in the Red Sea off Warner Point. Vanguard has identified the ship as sailing under the flag of Tanzania, while shipping website MarineTraffic says it is owned by an Egyptian operator. In its statement, Yemen's ministry of transport referred to Tihama as a "Yemeni commercial ship", while earlier reports in Iranian media referred to it as "Saudi-affiliated". The pictures of the vessel, which were shared by Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency, have been verified as new and show no signs of AI-generation. item.title: Thailand suspends new gun permits after mass shooting
item.description:

========================================
Thailand suspends new gun permits after mass shooting - Published Thailand's government will immediately stop issuing gun permits after a shooting incident last week in which a 14-year-old killed eight people and himself. Existing gun owners are already banned from carrying their weapons in public. The South East Asian country has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in the region, with around 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, and high levels of gun crime. In response to the recent shooting, the prime minister has promised to pass tough new gun control laws with severe penalties, suspending new permits in the meantime. Last Friday, a pupil at Debsirin Nonthaburi School outside Bangkok shot his grandparents using a handgun owned by his grandfather, before opening fire at teachers and students at school, authorities say. Both grandparents, five staff members at the school and one 12-year-old girl died. Police believe the shooter may have taught himself to use a gun via social media. They say there is evidence that the boy watched violent content online, and that he showed a strong interest in learning how to handle guns. His consumption of this content as well as anxiety over studies and family issues might have also fuelled his actions, they add. Until further notice, no new permits to purchase or own guns will be issued. Existing purchase permits will not be renewed but it is unclear what will happen to existing gun ownership permits. Permits to carry guns were suspended in late 2023 - owners must keep their weapons at home or at a shooting range. The government is also considering measures to persuade the owners of an estimated four million unlicensed guns to hand them over in the wake of the school shooting. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has said the announced measures will remain in place as the government works to pass new gun control laws, with stronger controls and significantly harsher penalties. Gun control advocates have called for mental health assessments as part of the permit process, and for permits to be periodically re-evaluated. Anutin has said stricter ammunition controls are in his sights, while the education minister has proposed screening at the entrance of schools to stop students from bringing in weapons. - Published1 day ago - Published3 days ago

item.title: Libyan authorities battle big blaze at major oil refinery
item.description:

Libyan authorities battle big blaze at major oil refinery - Published Libyan emergency services have been battling to contain a huge blaze at a major oil plant after it was targeted by unknown attackers. The Zawiya refinery, west of the capital Tripoli, was hit in a drone strike on Monday evening - the third such incident in two days. The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said a tank containing about 4.5m litres of fuel was directly hit, triggering a huge fire that caused it to collapse. It said it was considering suspending operations if the attacks continued. There were no "serious injuries" from the fire, with most patients treated for smoke inhalation, Libya's Ambulance and Emergency Service said on Tuesday. The Zawiya refinery is the largest operational facility in Libya, with an output of 120,000 barrels per day. The NOC condemned similar attacks in past days in Zawiya, including two drone strikes on a naphtha reservoir and a water desalination plant. It called on the authorities to investigate who was behind the violence. The attacks have highlighted continuing instability in Libya, which has been split in two since a civil war broke out after the ousting of former leader Muammar Gaddafi. Colonel Gaddafi seized power in 1969 and ruled autocratically for four decades until he was toppled and killed in 2011 in a rebellion assisted by Western military intervention Since his fall, rival power centres, one based in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, and one in the west in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, have been jostling for political and military dominance. item.title: Australia PM under fire for remarks on Japanese counterpart's melon gifts
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0jl6ewvq42o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Australia PM under fire for remarks on Japanese counterpart's melon gifts - Published Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is under fire for comments he made about two melons gifted to him by his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi, after a former Japanese envoy called it an insult. During an appearance on the Bush Deep podcast, Albanese gestured near his chest while referring to the crown melons, calling them "pretty strange" gifts that "ended up being quite good". That episode, which aired in July, had already landed the PM in hot water because of "inappropriate" comments he made about popstar Kylie Minogue. Opposition leaders are now demanding he apologise to Takaichi, but Albanese's position is that it was the host who made the joke, not him, the BBC understands. While discussing the melons Takaichi's team had presented to Albanese during her visit to Australia in May, the host of Bush Deep, comedian Nikki Osborne, quipped: "She brought two... She just came in looking like Pamela Anderson." "She brought two, and they are beautiful," Albanese responded. The exchange, which drew relatively little interest when the episode aired, has resurfaced after Tokyo's former ambassador to Canberra Shingo Yamagami labelled Albanese's comments a "sexist joke" and said they "betrayed the close bond" between Japan and Australia. "The last thing [Takaichi] expected was to be so casually mocked by the trusted leader of Japan's special strategic partner," he wrote in an opinion piece published by The Australian on Monday. Crown melons are the "most prized fruit" in Japan and "treasured as something special", Yamagami added, noting that a single melon costs more than 30,000 yen ($188). "So, prime minister, please enjoy Japan's sweet and juicy melons without thinking about a woman's anatomy, and instead focus on what our two countries must do together," he said. During his two-year stint in Australia, Yamagami had a notably frosty relationship with some members of Albanese's Labor Party over disagreements regarding China. An opposition MP asked Albanese on Tuesday if he would apologise for the "foul-mouthed, classless comments about women", to which the prime minister said he "rejected the assertion of the question". He went on: "Australia and Japan have never been closer. My government has taken our special strategic partnership to new heights." Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor on Monday also criticised the gaffe as "insulting", and demanded that Albanese make a personal apology. Several Labor ministers have jumped to Albanese's defence, saying the former envoy and the media have misinterpreted his comments. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the remarks "were not intended to be interpreted the way that our political opponents and some media outlets are reporting". Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek called it "a completely unnecessary interpretation of what the prime minister said". "I think people watching it for themselves can make their own minds up," Plibersek told Australia's Channel Seven. Plibersek had earlier defended Albanese's controversial remarks about Minogue as nothing more than a sign that he was a fan. The prime minister drew a wave of condemnation early last month after Osborne asked him on the podcast whether he would "shag, marry or date" Kylie Minogue, actress Nicole Kidman or entertainer Rhonda Burchmore, to which he replied "Kylie, clearly... all of the above". Albanese later issued a public apology, saying: "I apologise unequivocally for the comments". Osborne, who is best known for posting crude comedy sketches on YouTube, launched her podcast series earlier this year. Her podcast site describes her as a "wildly inappropriate journalist" who asks "questions no one else would dare".

item.title: Canada flight cancelled after child refuses to wear seat belt
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj6307x3wdgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Canada flight cancelled after child refuses to wear seat belt - Published The cancellation of a flight in Canada after a child refused to wear a seat belt has reignited a debate about the etiquette and safety procedures relating to children travelling on planes. The Porter Airlines flight, which was preparing to depart from Victoria to Toronto on 6 August had to return to the terminal as a "young child was standing in their seat and would not secure their seat belt", the airline said. The delay meant the flight could not depart before the runway closed after midnight so passengers had to be rebooked on a flight the following day. The incident has split opinion about how children should be treated in such situations and how airlines should respond. Regarding the child's behaviour, Porter Airlines said "attempts by the accompanying parent and crew to address this were unsuccessful". "The aircraft could not take off in this unsafe condition, so the crew elected to return to the terminal and have the two passengers disembark," it added. Child aviation safety expert Lia Tuso told the BBC the Porter crew were protecting the safety of the passengers on the flight with their decision to stop the flight, as well as the child. "Unrestrained children can become projectiles," Tuso said, similar to unrestrained items of luggage, which can fly into passengers in the event of turbulence, especially during takeoff and landing. The incident has led to a debate online over how tolerant airlines should be to travelling families, and how strictly parents should enforce airline rules. Some have said it was an example of what happens when parents are too "gentle" on their children. The Fox News morning programme debated it, with co-host Charles Hurt saying he supported physical discipline. "We've all been those parents," he said. "But this is beyond the pale." Other people have pointed out that sometimes children are afraid of flying and are not trying to be disruptive. One passenger on the Porter Airlines plane, Aryeh Kozuch, told CBC News the child had not been unruly but had seemed scared. "They just kept hiding under their seat. If they got forced into [being] strapped in, they just kind of slid out underneath." Many have questioned why the whole flight had to be disrupted for one child and said the family should have been removed. This is what happened in 2018, when a father and daughter were filmed being ejected from a Southwest Airlines flight from Chicago to Atlanta. According to a passenger who filmed the incident, the child had settled down from a tantrum, and had been quietly seated in her seat for more than five minutes before the airline's crew informed the father they would be removed from the flight. The airline involved, Southwest, said initial reports indicated "a conversation escalated onboard between the crew and a customer travelling with a small child". After a similar incident in 2012, the family who were kicked off appeared on NBC's Today Show to accuse the airline of showing a lack of humanity. JetBlue, the airline involved, said it "had customers that did not comply with crew member instructions for a prolonged time period". It added: "The captain elected to remove the customers involved for the safety of all customers and crew members on board.'' item.title: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3q5vl581wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots - Published US President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) shots. "Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today," Trump said. "In those times, people were much healthier and of course the high rates of autism now observed did not exist." The president has long cast doubt on the safety of MMR vaccines, but multiple studies have found no connection between the shots and autism. Medical experts have criticised the new order and said it could reduce vaccination rates and expose children to harmful diseases. The order also recommends that the number of childhood vaccines drop to 11 from the existing 18 recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP). Trump's order serves as guidance, not a mandate, since shots required for school attendance are set at the state level, rather than by the federal government. The immunisations recommended for all children under the order are for measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella or chicken pox. "We're reducing them," Trump said. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor." The president suggested the MMR vaccine could be "quite lethal" if given at once. He compared it to pouring a bottle of soda into a child's body. According to the FDA, external, a single dose of MMR is 0.5ml. When a reporter asked for evidence of the "lethal" claim, Trump said: "What I've heard is that there are some people that say it is that way." According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), external, the MMR vaccine carries a very small risk of febrile seizures for young children. Those with health issues, including severe allegeric reactions or weakened immune systems, are advised to consult with healthcare providers before taking the shots. The agency says "most people who get MMR vaccine do not have any serious problems with it", and that getting the vaccine "is much safer than getting measles, mumps, or rubella". According to the CDC, there is "no published scientific evidence that shows any benefit in separating the combination MMR vaccine into three individual shots". Experts say that allowing time between jabs means children are more likely to contract diseases in the interim or that they are more likely to miss appointments if there are multiple shots. Dr William Schaffner of the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine in Nashville told the BBC the increased number of visits would be harder for parents and providers to track and would add to the expense without any scientific benefit. Since taking office in 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F Kennedy Jr has sought to change and loosen vaccine regulations. During a tense 20-minute interview on CNN last week, Kennedy insisted he had "never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine". He said the proposed changes were meant to give parents choice, not prohibit access to childhood vaccines. Trump administration officials have said the order means children in the US would receive much less than the 72 shots recommended under the previous vaccine schedule, a figure that assumes annual flu and Covid-19 doses. Dr Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said Trump's executive order was "dangerous" and not based on "gold-standard science". "Delaying or skipping shots is risky, especially as measles continues to spread and children go back to school," Racine said. Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, who was the deciding vote in the Senate to confirm Kennedy as health secretary, also admonished Trump's executive order on Monday, labelling it "wrong". "The President does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy, a physician, wrote on X. "Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism." Experts fear that if parents refrain from getting their children vaccinated as a result of the discredited idea that childhood vaccines are linked to autism, it risks the re-emergence of diseases like measles. Multiple studies have found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism. A recent high-quality study from Denmark in 2019 looked at 657,461 children and concluded that the data did not support the MMR vaccine causing or triggering autism. On its website, the CDC recommends that two doses of the combined MMR vaccine be given to children, starting with the first dose at 12-15 months and the second between the ages of four and six. How often and how many vaccines children in the US receive is based on the times when vaccines will work best with their immune systems and when they are most vulnerable to certain diseases, according to the AAP. There is no medical reason to delay or skip recommended immunisations, the AAP says. Trump's order also calls for the development of alternatives to aluminium in vaccines, and to test if those alternatives are safer and more effective. But the AAP, external says studies have found no significant health risks associated with the tiny amounts of aluminium salts in vaccines. Small amounts of aluminium salts - which are found naturally in soil, water and foods - have been used in some vaccines for decades in order to boost the body's immune response. That means lesser quantities of the vaccine and fewer doses are needed, according to AAP. - Published23 September 2025 - Published23 September 2025 - Published10 hours ago

Jackie, the famous California bald eagle, dies after weeks of intensive care - Published Jackie, a bald eagle in California who became an online star, died on Monday after receiving weeks of veterinary treatment. Jackie was being cared for by Ojai Raptor Center, a wildlife rehabilitation organisation, after she was attacked by other eagles. The bird had underlying health issues that caused anaemia and weight loss. "Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists," Ojai Raptor Center said in a statement. A livestream featuring the Big Bear Valley nest of Jackie and her partner, Shadow, has hundreds of thousands of subscribers. The Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam, run by the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley in California, amassed a loyal following and Jackie was frequently spotted in the area since she hatched in the spring of 2012. Jackie and Shadow had been mates since 2018, the Friends of Big Bear Valley website said. "Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her," the Ojai Raptor Center said. "We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her. "We are working closely with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and will provide a more comprehensive statement including additional information on her treatments and test results." Jackie's remains have been transferred to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the Ojai Raptor Center said.

item.title: The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/basketball/articles/ckg3enx6rj6o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA - Published The WNBA is still in the midst of its 2026 season and yet it is next year's Draft for North America's top women's basketball league that is dominating the headlines. Why? Because some former men's NBA players have declared they will enter for selection - citing the current eligibility guidelines, or lack of, for transgender women players. "I'm officially declaring myself a WNBA prospect," said Enes Kanter Freedom, who played 11 seasons in the NBA. It is the latest development in a story ignited by a comment made by Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham, who said she wanted to protect young girls "who shouldn't have to go against biological men" in sport. Her words have instigated protests - albeit not grand in scale - on both sides of the argument, and once again catapulted the debate around transgender women in sport into the spotlight. How did we get here? Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the topic of "protecting" women's sports. The Indiana Fever guard said she had received criticism from people who believed she "hated" transgender people, something she denied. She said she wanted to "extend love" to everyone, but added: "I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men." She later doubled down on her comments, saying it was "common sense", external to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports. Her words quickly moved beyond basketball and into a wider political debate in the United States. President Donald Trump expressed his support for Cunningham, while vice-president JD Vance said she was "inspiring". Though the 29-year-old later said she is "not a very political person", her remarks have followed her around the country. Competing rallies from critics and supporters were organised at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests. The scale of the debate in the media, online and in politics was striking given no openly transgender woman is due to play, or has ever played, in the WNBA. What do the rules say? The WNBA operates under a collective bargaining agreement (CBA), a deal negotiated between the league and its players association (WNBPA), setting rules on matters including player salary caps, revenue sharing, benefits and overall league operations. On player eligibility, the CBA states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." The WNBA has yet to comment publicly on the row since Cunningham's comments but league commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week in which she said the matter would be discussed at an upcoming pre-arranged meeting with team presidents. In the memo, seen by the Associated Press, external, Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league". She added: "Our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities." However, the lack of detail in the league's eligibility criteria has been brought to light by Kanter Freedom, who finished his playing career with the Boston Celtics in 2022. "If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," he wrote on Instagram, external. Kanter Freedom, who has previously spoken out about human rights violations in China and Turkey, among other issues, added: "I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices. "I'm simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone - the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for." A day after Kanter Freedom's 'announcement', Royce White - who made three appearances in the NBA as a player and is now a Republican Senate candidate - said he would also declare for the Draft, adding: "I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball." Whether the vagueness of the rules are by design to leave it open to transgender women or a sign of an oversight that genuinely needs tightening up is not clear. BBC Sport has contacted Cunningham's representatives, the WNBA and WNBPA for comment. What has the reaction been? Cunningham's comments have become a flashpoint inside a league which has a long history of player activism on issues including race, gender equality and LGBTQ+ rights. The players' association did not mention Cunningham by name when it eventually addressed the debate. In a statement the WNBPA denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" and reaffirmed its commitment to "justice, equity, diversity and inclusion". It called on fans to report abusive behaviour at games and added that it would continue to have "hard" conversations but it "will not be used as political pawns". There is strong feeling on both sides of the argument. Minnesota Lynx head coach and president Cheryl Reeve, who said: "I come from a space of inclusion. "The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports." Reeve wore a "Trans Kids Belong" T-shirt before Minnesota played Indiana earlier this month and was seen speaking to Cunningham on court before the game. Cunningham later said the pair had exchanged their perspectives and that the conversation ended with "love and respect". Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams said she would welcome a transgender athlete "on my team or against my team, any time". Last month, the WNBA suspended Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton from attending the team's next five home games after an exchange with two fans, who were sat courtside displaying signs thanking Cunningham for "speaking up for girls". Keaton reportedly confronted the teenage fans and admonished them during the game. The Storm have since apologised. As for Cunningham, the attention has increasingly become an unwelcome distraction. Having defended her original comments, she said recently that she now wanted the conversation to return to what was happening on court. "I want to get back to basketball, it's always been about basketball" she said, arguing that the standard of play in the WNBA was being overshadowed by issues away from the game. But that may prove difficult, as pressure grows on the league to clarify exactly who is eligible to play. What are the rules in other sports? In recent years, many governing bodies in sport have amended their rules about the inclusion of transgender athletes at the elite level, moving more towards restrictions. Athletics, cycling and aquatics, for example, have implemented outright bans on transgender women taking part in women's events. In March, it was announced that the women's category of Olympic sports will be limited to biological females from the LA Olympic Games in 2028. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) says eligibility will be determined by a "once-in-a-lifetime" sex test, which would prevent transgender women and those with differences in sexual development (DSD) who have gone through male puberty from competing. In the United States, transgender women and girls are banned from competing in women's sports categories in schools, universities and the grassroots level. That was part of an executive order - titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" - signed by President Trump last year. It does not cover professional sport.
