item.title: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn9n8pqglg4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides - Published At 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts. They promised he wouldn't have to waste years on building a relationship that had no future. They offered to introduce him to a demure, devoted woman. "The matchmakers said that girls from Guizhou are frugal," Wang says. "They told me they are good at running a household, able to do housework, and their families are very poor, so after marrying into your family, they would settle down and live a life with you." So Wang travelled to Guiyang, a city in the southwestern province of Guizhou, in the hope of finding his soulmate. He thought he had, when he was matched with a woman who seemed to tick every box. They had only met a few times before they married. Then, almost as quickly as his new life had begun, it was over. "My whole family has been thrown into chaos," he says, shaking his head. He is still picking up the pieces more than a year after he discovered that everything he had been told by his wife was a lie. She was a former karaoke hostess who'd been married three times, had three children, a serious sexually transmitted disease and was deeply in debt. She had even lied about her age. He is fighting for a divorce and cannot return home to his old life - at least until he can recoup some of his life savings, which he says he paid to the agency within hours of being introduced to several potential matches. "My parents blame me. I have insomnia and anxiety. I can't focus on work." Wang's story is an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis that has long been in the making in China. For decades, China's Communist Party decreed that couples could have only one child. They reversed course in January 2016 but by then the "one-child" policy, coupled with a preference for boys, had produced a shrinking pool of women and a stark gender imbalance. There are now 30 million more men than women in China – that's more than the male population of the UK, or the entire population of Australia. This has left men like Wang, who are in their late 30s and who live in smaller cities or far-flung, rural areas, with few options. Women in these places can afford to be choosy as they know they are in demand. "The requirements for men are very high in my city. You need to have a car, a house and your family should preferably run a business," he says. Many families also demand a high "bride price", a longstanding Chinese custom where the groom's family gives money to the bride. In parts of China, where men far outnumber women, this has become a significant financial burden. Hence the appeal of matchmaking agencies like the ones in Guizhou, which are proposing a one-stop, quick solution - or "flash marriages". Matchmaking agencies are hardly new in China, but many seem to be finding vulnerable targets in men who are struggling to find partners as they grow older. So much so that state media recently reported that the industry had seen "rapid growth" which had "bred illegal practices and chaos". It's hard to determine the scale of such fraud across China but it has grown enough to draw the attention of Chinese officials. Between January 2024 and March 2025, prosecutors handled cases involving 1,546 individuals for crimes related to the matchmaking industry. This month, five separate authorities jointly launched a nationwide crackdown on the matchmaking industry after the issue generated "widespread public concern". In one case, a matchmaking agency reportedly used karaoke waitresses as bait to defraud 128 victims of more than 2.5 million yuan (£274,000, $371,000). "I think the government could introduce industry-specific regulations targeting flash marriage scams," Fan Binghe, from the Nanjing Office of the Beijing Jingshi law firm, told the BBC. Although Guiyang has become synonymous with this booming "flash marriage" market, there is little to suggest it is a romantic hub. The agency offices sit in a dense warren of buildings above a shopping precinct, where vendors sell local fruit and workers queue for takeaway sour soup rice noodles. Wang, however, was convinced he could trust them after the company told him they would do a full background check and that he would be entitled to compensation if he was the victim of fraud. So he paid up and the introductions began. He met seven women in various "blind date" rooms over a few days while being carefully supervised by agency staff. He asked questions about where they came from, if they'd been married before and if they had any kids. He set his heart on the eighth woman he met. He was hoping to meet someone who hadn't been married before, with no children and who was just a little younger than him. "She also dressed very simply," he recalls. "She looked introverted and honest." They met four or five times for just eight to 10 minutes each time. He says they had been under strict instructions not to exchange phone numbers or any details on private messages, or they would be fined. After two or three days he decided she was the one and he agreed to pay her a substantial bride price. "I spent more than 300,000 yuan [$44,000]," he says, with a pile of well-thumbed legal papers in hand to prove it. "If you include the wedding banquet and everything else, I spent around 400,000 to 500,000 yuan." The whole process was documented by the matchmaking agency in a series of glossy photos, which they also use to advertise their services on Chinese social media. In the video the couple are holding hands on a red carpet and smiling while romantic music plays in the background. Just months into the marriage, debt collectors started calling, alleging she owed them money. Wang grew suspicious and wanted to know what else she had kept hidden. He checked her phone and found details of her former life, her birth certificate and former marriage documents. When he confronted her, she offered him a divorce, but refused to return a single penny of the bride price. He says he tried to hunt down the agency responsible for his marriage, but when he returned to their offices, they had packed up and disappeared. From his rented flat in Guiyang, just across from the main district which houses most of these agencies, Wang now spends his time making social media videos trying to warn other men about what can go wrong. In Guiyang, it is difficult to find an agency where the staff is willing to talk. One agency boss agreed to talk to us in their offices – although his business partner later asked us to leave. Inside there was a red carpet littered with fake petals ready for a proposal. He told us a couple had pledged to marry just hours before we arrived. "There's a huge market for flash marriages in China. It only really emerged over the last two or three years," he told us. The agencies claim families here did not strictly adhere to the one-child policy, which means the area has a larger pool of women. "Even if a family had two or three daughters, they would keep trying for a son," one of them told the BBC. They say they are now trying to match these women with men from central provinces – like Wang who lives in Hebei – who are relatively wealthy but have few women around them. "Our clients are free to choose whoever they like. The purpose of our business is to help people find someone they genuinely want to be with." One of the advertisements assures their prospective clients that "Three days with the right introduction can beat three years of dating". Wang now spends his time trying to help other victims of similar spiels. His rented flat is full of men who are either searching for the owners of the agency who scammed them, or are trying to recoup their losses from their wives who ran off after only a few weeks of marriage. On a fold-up bed by the window, 59-year-old Xu Rulin from Jiangxi province pulls his carefully collated evidence out of a red plastic shopping bag. He spent nearly 500,000 yuan trying to find his son a wife through a "flash marriage" agency. Together they travelled to Guiyang - more than 1,000km away - and his son wed just seven days after he first met his bride in a "blind date" room. Xu says after the marriage was registered, she demanded they buy her an iPhone and transfer around 20,000 yuan to help her with her business. She also asked for 120,000 yuan for a wedding dress and jewellery, he claims. "All I wanted was for her to genuinely settle down and live with us," he told us. "She said she wanted a house and I agreed to buy one for them. It was all agreed." But he says she ran away after living with them for less than two weeks. She has been detained by the police, and the couple have been able to get divorced. He says the owners of the matchmaking company were also arrested in January this year, but he is still in Guiyang trying to recover some of the losses. The agency manager the BBC spoke to admitted there were no formal background checks on their clients. "The women are introduced by local matchmakers who already know them very well. They know their family background because they're often from the same village. The male's matchmaker also usually knows the man very well." They would not say how much their services cost because that information was "confidential". He did say that if the information provided by either side is not truthful, then the client is entitled to get their money back. "I'd say more than 90% of what our clients tell us here is true," he claimed. "We have a saying here in China. One rotten mouse dropping spoils the whole pot of soup. That's exactly what it's like. We regularly attend meetings with the local police. If a matchmaking agency is found to be involved in marriage fraud, it will be held legally responsible." This brings little comfort for those who have lost whatever money they had saved. "I never imagined that with the agency charging such a high service fee, a local matchmaker in her hometown checking her background and the company offering so many guarantees, that the women's information would turn out to be completely fake," Wang says. He is almost resigned now to his losses. And he blames himself for falling for the scam: "Only women with problems would agree to these kind of flash marriages." He has kneeled at the police offices in Guiyang pleading for them to help him get his money back and he has even travelled to Beijing to urge the authorities to do more to combat this type of crime. These cases are difficult to prosecute, says Fan Binghe, the lawyer who has handled many. For one, Chinese law has no specific criminal offence which covers this kind of marriage fraud, and so to bring criminal charges, a victim has to establish that the aim of their spouse was always to take their money. "In cases I've handled, suspects often argue that they genuinely intended to marry and live a good life but realised they were incompatible, had conflicts, and decided to end the relationship," he says. "In situations like that, the line becomes blurred. Relationship issues are difficult to disprove." Even harder is getting money back from sham matchmaking agencies which often shut up shop as soon as they have made enough cash. Wang has managed to get some money back, but not all. "After going through something like this, I don't even know if I can still get married. It was already hard for me to find someone. And now I've spent so much money. I won't consider it now." Wang's life, and the life of the men in the apartment, all appear to be in limbo. "It has taken almost two years, and even now I still don't know when I can divorce her," he says, surrounded by his legal paperwork. "I don't know when this will be resolved, so I can restart a normal life. It feels endless."

item.title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgxjn92x9jo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame? - Published After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why? A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising. But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer. The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors. In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a €150,000 (£128,000) fine, if convicted. Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Étape forest in the Vosges region. "Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est Républicain, the newspaper that reported the story. Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts. "I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction. The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame. The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues. But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances. "The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying. Working out how a fire started is, unsurprisingly, not easy. "In periods of drought such as this one, all you need is a simple lighter," explains Eric Dufayet, an officer who investigates fires. Once a fire is out, Eric's first task is to map its outline along the edge of the burnt vegetation, then trace it back to its point of origin. If the wind has been steady, that outline often forms a "V" shape. From there, his team works backwards along the path the flames took. "If someone deliberately starts a fire, they may not have used only one device," he says. It improves the chances of a DNA or fingerprint sample being found. Experts believe arson accounts for only a small fraction of fires. Most are believed to be accidental, with sparks potentially coming from construction work, faulty electrical equipment, cigarette butts and barbecues. "With cigarettes, it's called the '30' rule," says Eric Dufayet. To start a fire, he explains, there must be "a temperature of at least 30C (86F), a maximum of 30% humidity, wind of less than 30km/h (19mph), and at least 30% of the cigarette unburnt." In the current drought, he says it is even easier. If those conditions are met, a fire can easily spread, and fast. According to Michel Lejoyeux, a professor of psychiatry and addictive behaviour at Paris 7 University, people who start fires fall into three categories: those who are careless, those who benefit - with an insurance payout, for example - and pyromaniacs. "The pyromaniac doesn't get money, has no spirit of revenge, has no utility of the fire, but he likes the fire," he says. However, pyromania is a rare psychiatric disorder that Lejoyeux says is very difficult to diagnose, and accounts for few arson convictions. Lawyer Muriel Gestas, who has handled several such cases, says some firefighters alleged to have started fires may have wanted to be seen as saviours. For others - notably volunteers earning tax-free overtime - the motive may be financial. Amid concerns over how officials are pursuing suspects, broader worries about wildfires are far from abating. Forecasts suggest France's next heatwave is only days away. President Emmanuel Macron says criticism should not be the priority right now. "We will have to replant and rebuild a different kind of forest because we must adapt to the structural conditions of climate change," he said this week. "The time for reviewing lessons learned will come," he insisted. "In the meantime, the country must remain united." Even so, the damage these fires have inflicted on the environment, hundreds of homes, tourism, local businesses and air quality has left the French public with a lot of questions.

item.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9q94lxqrzzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope - Published "Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat. Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement. Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater. Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland – in the south-western corner of Australia – is one of the few places they remain. As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival. Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency. This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change. Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion. Australia has long been celebrated as a nature haven, home to some of the world's most unique plant and animal species. More than 80% cannot be found anywhere else. But it has arguably become the extinction capital of the world, losing roughly four species every decade - and the decline is only worsening. Dedicated volunteers and under-funded conservationists have been slowing the army of increasing threats, but experts fear that without urgent action and political courage, the biodiversity Australia says it loves is headed for a bloodbath. "It's not even a case of imagining it, it's happening in front of our own eyes," Professor Euan Ritchie tells the BBC. The many threats driving extinction If spotting a rare creature in the wild wasn't challenging enough, the numbat is a squirrel-sized camouflage connoisseur, explains Dr Tony Friend, the godfather of conservation in the state of Western Australia. "They just slept in today," jokes Rob McLean, president of the Numbat Taskforce, a volunteer group which makes a lot of Tony's thinly-resourced work possible. For two weeks each spring, as the young start venturing from their burrows, this team drives a daily circuit and records every numbat spotted. They log GPS coordinates, measure the distance to the road, and use a complicated equation to estimate the density of the animals in these woods and, from that, broader population health. One person sits in concentrated silence at each window, another perched in the back of the pick-up truck, ducking for the occasional limb branching from trees which rise around us. Through the trunks, we get the occasional glimpse of the razed farmland which tightly fences this pocket of protected woodland. On the side of one trail is a machine which detects and sprays feral cats and foxes with poison, another reminder of the perils numbats face. "This year's been a bit of a feast," Rob admits. For hours on end, we cruise around, seeing parrots, wallabies, a goanna and a couple of echidnas - but no numbats. Tony arrived at Dryandra back in the 80s to find a numbat population fewer than 50. Many of the culprits then were the same as those still driving extinctions across the nation today. Swathes of critical habitat are being cleared for development or industries like farming, mining and timber. Leaving a trail of destruction in their wake are introduced pests: fire ants, cane toads, rabbits, foxes, feral cats. Invasive weeds like lantana are choking the Australian bush, chlamydia has sent koalas to the edge of existence across much of the country, while the skin-eating chytrid fungus has caused seven frog extinctions here and counting. The changing climate is creating unliveable conditions for some species, like native flying foxes which are dropping out of trees in their thousands due to extreme temperatures. For others it is eliminating their food or their homes. Climate change is also driving natural disasters which fry and drown both plants and animals with now frightening regularity. The infamous Black Summer bushfires of 2019-20, for example, killed an estimated three billion animals. The successive years of record-breaking flooding which followed were so widespread it's impossible to estimate the impact on wildlife. Many species once abundant across the continent are now isolated to increasingly small and disjointed patches, each impact compounding and leaving them more vulnerable to the next. There are small, yet determined, efforts to slow the momentum of decline. As a young numbat scoffs his breakfast – custard with "termite sprinkles" – at Perth Zoo, a keeper explains how this stud's upcoming release at Dryandra will help boost genetic diversity. "When you get that feedback: your babies have got babies, it's very satisfying," Vicki Power says. Breeding programmes like this have also made setting up additional populations of an array of threatened species possible. But many cannot survive in the true wild, where large-scale predator control remains an endless battle, and are instead sent to fenced nature reserves, themselves high-maintenance undertakings facing problems like in-breeding and overpopulation. Habitat protection or restoration projects have been ramping up, but they are not keeping pace with destruction, particularly in the most critical areas. Scientists are also trying to fight disease, though that's an expensive and laborious endeavour, which for most species buys only a little more time. Others are preserving genetic material in case we ever work out how to resurrect species from the dead. A hundred species lost - and counting Scientists agree that we're living though the world's sixth mass extinction event, the first caused by humans. But Australia is at the front of this trend. It leads the world in mammal extinctions, and medals when it comes to the loss of other species classes too. "Despite Australia being one of the wealthiest countries per capita in the world and having more than its fair share of world-leading scientists… we have a truly awful record of conserving species," Ritchie says. "And things aren't getting better." The Australian government's official extinctions list sits at 67, but researchers are confident at least 100 plant and animal species have been lost forever. They suspect the true figure is far higher. The country is still discovering species which have already been wiped out. Though the rate of extinction in Australia has stayed stable, at around four per decade, the number of threatened species is still climbing quickly, and the deterioration of many is only gathering speed. This trajectory has some scary flow-on effects, experts warn. Australia's biodiversity "underpins everything", ecologist Jack Pascoe says. Think food production, tourism, construction – much of the economy. Potential scientific breakthroughs could be stymied: in medicine, agriculture and even climate change adaptation. And for First Nations Australians, the decline also threatens their culture. "We think of ourselves as custodians of all life on Earth… so there's a much more personal and social feeling of loss that comes when these things are not doing well or we lose them forever," Pascoe, a man from the Yuin Aboriginal nation, says. Decades of failures Though environment protection is a state responsibility, the federal government oversees matters of national importance. Labor took office in 2022, promising no new extinctions under its watch, and it has sought to make nature protection a defining feature of its second term. "It's well understood that nature is facing many challenges in the world today, both here in Australia, and overseas… we are losing biodiversity at an alarming rate," Environment Minister Murray Watt told the BBC in a statement. His party has significantly increased Australia's emissions reduction efforts and massively boosted renewable energy projects. There is some praise for their work on drawing critically endangered mammals back from the brink. And the passage of revamped environment laws last year was heralded as the most significant reform in a generation. The country also has an ambitious goal to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. But there's limited optimism that this will be a real turning point. The new laws are only the scaffolding of change. The substance of it is still being worked out – in the form of National Environmental Standards (NES) and a federal watchdog to enforce them. And many in the sector say the problem is not so much the regulatory tools available, but rather the political will to use them. Successive governments have failed to adequately protect the environment over the past 30 years, Australia's longest serving environment minister tells the BBC. That includes his own administration. "We should have done more too," says Robert Hill, who lead the last major reforms in 1999 under John Howard's conservative coalition. Many of the challenges of his era still haunt leaders today. The nation's wealth has largely been built off the back of its natural resources – often at the expense of the environment. Those riches still underpin the economy and help fund government spending on essentials like healthcare and housing. Then there's the added pressure applied by industry and the competing interests of states - whose stake in regulatory controls blurs the lines of accountability and increases bureaucratic hurdles. These battles leave even the toughest environmental advocates within governments bruised. For example, the Albanese government last year rushed through laws protecting salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officials, silencing opposition from within and ignoring advice from its own department concerning the impact of the A$1.4bn (£733m; $989m) industry on the survival of the Maugean Skate, an endangered ray. "The axe falls on the environmental outcome if there's the alternative of an economic one," Hill says. "Even if [the federal government] does want to act, it's still got to have the political strength to turn its aspirations into reality." There is also a belief that greater regulation alone will achieve little. Too much conservation work currently relies on philanthropists' cash and devoted volunteers, those in the sector say, and much more languishes on the to-do list due to a lack of money. The federal government directly spends about A$700m on nature protection, a fraction of the A$33bn – or 1% of GDP – conservationists say it should be. That is an eyebrow-raising figure, people like Paul Elton concede, but one they argue is reasonable. According to his research – which the government disputes – more than A$26bn is still being spent on subsidies for things like mining, intensive agriculture or fuel despite Australia signing global pledges to wind them back. "For every dollar the government is spending on positive biodiversity conservation action, there's A$26 being spent on subsidies that are causing harm to nature," he tells the BBC. "That's a pretty stark imbalance." Minister Watt didn't directly respond to questions about conservationists' demands, but said: "We remain committed to long-term environmental recovery, in partnership with state and local governments, community and environmental groups." Though public sentiment is shifting, there's scepticism the government will prioritise the environment amid competing demands and compounding crises until voters force them to do so. "The community will say to you, we should spend a lot of money on the environment. And then if you say, 'Well, what are you prepared to sacrifice to ensure that funding base?', then they're no longer interested," Hill says. In the face of so many challenges and what they see as little progress, advocates admit it's hard to hang on to hope. "We know what the problems are. We know how to address them. We know when we spend money on the environment, it pays back many times over," Ritchie, a mammal ecologist, says. "It's like being a doctor and seeing all these sick people in the community and you know how to fix them, but no one will let you do that." Small wins, like the future of the numbat, keep them fighting. There are now around 3,000 nationwide, and in Dryandra numbers have increased ten-fold. The animal has recently been taken off the international endangered species list and is now classified as near-threatened. It takes five hours, but finally synchronised cries of excitement come from the driver's seat and the back of the pick-up truck. The cause of the commotion stands frozen and alert at the end of a hollowing log. "It's not a competition," Rob says. Chuckling, he points at his rival spotter: "But I beat him by a second." The dam has broken. Over the next little while we see eight numbats, including two pairs of babies, blinking at us in the dusky light. This year's full count, Tony later tells me, is one of the best yet. "But I remind people they're not out of the woods yet," Tony says. The relief at the numbat's revival is tempered by worry this will make it harder to access the funding and support needed to cement those gains. The woylie, or brush-tailed bettong, is a cautionary tale. It recovered slightly and was taken off the threatened list only to be added again a decade later, in a worse state. "We can't walk away," Tony says, "and say 'no, they're fine,' you know?" "It's got to be accepted that continued work is needed to keep that animal on the planet." Watch: Was Trump smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck? Donald Trump secretly switched planes when he was returning from a Nato meeting last month in order to avoid a threat to his life from Iran, US media has reported. The president boarded Air Force One in Ankara, Turkey, on 8 July before being transported to another aircraft with the help of a catering truck, the Washington Post said. He was then seen disembarking Air Force One in the UK, before boarding his newer, Qatari-gifted jet and returning to the US. Trump spoke to journalists during his flight to the US but did not say whether he had been moved to a different plane.
